## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Sessions 2-3: ordered outcomes and their assumption
- Today: **nominal** outcomes, with no ordering: place of delivery
- By the end you can:
  - fit `nnet::multinom` and choose a **reference category**
  - read **relative risk ratios** and test them
  - get **predicted probabilities**
:::

# Topic 1 — The model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## A set of logistic models against a reference

::: {.eq}
log [ P(Y = j) / P(Y = Home) ] = β~0j~ + β~1j~ x~1~ + …    for j = PHC, Public, Private
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **K − 1 equations** (3 for 4 places), each comparing a category with the **reference**
- **Every predictor has a different coefficient in each equation**
- exp(β~j~) is a **relative risk ratio** (an odds ratio versus the reference)
- Fitted jointly by maximum likelihood: the probabilities add to 1
:::

## Fit it

```{r}
mat$delivery <- relevel(mat$delivery, ref = "Home")
mn <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + education + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
round(exp(coef(mn)[, "wealth"]), 2)
```

::: {.key}
Each **wealth quintile** multiplies the odds of delivering in a **private hospital rather than at home** by **`r round(exp(coef(mn)[, "wealth"]), 2)[3]`**, in a **public hospital** by `r round(exp(coef(mn)[, "wealth"]), 2)[2]`, in a **PHC** by `r round(exp(coef(mn)[, "wealth"]), 2)[1]`. Wealth pulls women **away from home, and most strongly towards private care**.
:::

# Topic 2 — Tests and tables {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## The output has no p-values

```{r}
s <- summary(mn); z <- s$coefficients / s$standard.errors
round(2 * pnorm(-abs(z)), 4)[, c("wealth", "anc_visits", "residenceRural")]
```

Compute **z = coefficient / SE** and the two-sided p-value. For a variable with several coefficients (education has 3 per equation), use a **likelihood-ratio test** of the **whole** variable:

```{r}
mn0 <- nnet::multinom(delivery ~ wealth + anc_visits + residence + tribal, data = mat, trace = FALSE)
anova(mn0, mn)
```

## A table

```{r}
tbl_regression(mn, exponentiate = TRUE, include = wealth)
```

# Topic 3 — Using it {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Predicted probabilities

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(wealth = c(1, 5), education = factor("Secondary", levels = levels(mat$education)), anc_visits = 4, residence = factor("Urban", levels = c("Urban", "Rural")), tribal = factor("No", levels = c("No", "Yes")))
rownames(nd) <- c("poorest", "richest"); round(predict(mn, newdata = nd, type = "probs"), 2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- The poorest woman delivers mostly in **public hospitals or PHCs** (37% each) and only **4% in private care**
- The richest: **31% private**, 3% at home
- The **probabilities** tell the story more clearly than 9 odds ratios
:::

## The choice of reference

::: {.incremental}
- It changes **which comparisons** are shown, **not the model**: the fitted probabilities and log-likelihood are **identical**
- Choose a **large, meaningful** group (here Home) so the comparisons make sense
- Any other comparison (Private vs Public) = the **difference** of two coefficients; refit with another reference to get its CI
:::

## Pitfalls

::: {.bad}
- Reading RRRs as **risk ratios** when the outcome is common (they are odds-type ratios)
- **Sparse categories** (a few women in one place) make estimates unstable
- **Many parameters**: 3 equations x every predictor needs a large sample
- Ignoring the **independence of irrelevant alternatives** (adding or removing a category can change the others: be cautious with similar categories)
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q1", "In a multinomial model with four outcome categories and Home as the reference, how many coefficients does each predictor have?",
         c("One, which applies to every comparison",
           "Four, one for each category of the outcome",
           "Three, one for each comparison with the reference",
           "Zero, because multinomial models have no coefficients"), answer = 3,
         explain = "A K-category outcome yields K - 1 equations, so each predictor has K - 1 coefficients (here 3).")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q2", "The relative risk ratio for wealth is 2.76 for Private hospital versus Home. How should it be read?",
         c("Women in the richest quintile are 2.76 times as likely to be in any hospital",
           "Odds of private care rather than home rise 2.8-fold per quintile",
           "The probability of private care is 2.76 for each of the women studied",
           "Wealth raises the share of private deliveries by 2.76 percentage points"), answer = 2,
         explain = "The ratio compares the odds of one category with the reference, per unit of the predictor. It is not an absolute risk and not about all hospitals.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q3", "Why use a likelihood-ratio test to test education in a multinomial model?",
         c("The z-test cannot be calculated for any categorical variable at all",
           "The likelihood-ratio test is what gives the odds ratios in it",
           "The variable has several coefficients, tested all together",
           "A single z statistic would be zero for education"), answer = 3,
         explain = "A multi-level predictor has many coefficients (3 education dummies x 3 equations). A joint test compares the models with and without it.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q4", "What happens to the fitted probabilities if you change the reference category and refit?",
         c("They change, because the model fitted is a different one",
           "They are reversed in order, so that the last category comes first",
           "They can no longer be computed once the reference has changed",
           "They are the same: only how the comparisons are shown changes"), answer = 4,
         explain = "The reference only defines the parametrisation. Models with different references are equivalent: same likelihood, same predictions.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s4q5", "Which is a good reason to choose the multinomial model for an outcome with ordered categories?",
         c("Many predictors violate proportional odds and partial models fail",
           "The categories are few in number and the sample is large enough",
           "The researcher would prefer to avoid reporting odds ratios at all",
           "The reference category is hard to name for the outcome in question"), answer = 1,
         explain = "A multinomial model makes no ordering assumption, so it is a safe fallback when proportional odds clearly fails. The cost is many more parameters.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **K − 1 equations**, each against a **reference category**
- exp(β) = **relative risk ratio** (odds versus the reference)
- **z-tests** by hand; **likelihood-ratio** tests for multi-level variables
- The reference changes the **presentation**, not the **fit**; show **predicted probabilities**
:::
